l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Dr. Watson, a recently returned army surgeon whose health was ruined in Afghanistan, meets young Stamford in London while seeking inexpensive lodgings. Stamford introduces him to Sherlock Holmes, a chemically skilled and eccentric researcher working in a hospital laboratory. Holmes demonstrates a new test that detects hæmoglobin and identifies blood stains, then agrees to share a suite of rooms with Watson in Baker Street. Holmes also infers that Watson has been in Afghanistan, though he does not explain how.

l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Dr. Watson returns to England after serving as an army surgeon in Afghanistan, wounded at Maiwand and weakened by enteric fever. In London, he seeks cheaper lodgings and meets Sherlock Holmes through young Stamford, agreeing to inspect rooms with him in Baker Street.

l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Sherlock Holmes is introduced as an eccentric, highly knowledgeable investigator of chemistry and anatomy who works intermittently in a hospital laboratory. He discovers a reagent that reacts to hæmoglobin, demonstrates its use in detecting blood stains, and agrees to share lodgings with Dr. Watson. Holmes correctly infers that Watson has been in Afghanistan without explaining his method.

l: young Stamford, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Young Stamford, formerly a dresser under Dr. Watson at Barts, meets Watson in London and takes him to the hospital laboratory. He describes Sherlock Holmes’s scientific interests and peculiar habits, introduces the two men, and warns Watson that Holmes may be difficult to understand.

l: London, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: London is where Dr. Watson stays after returning from India and where his finances deteriorate while he lives in a private hotel in the Strand. He meets young Stamford at the Criterion Bar and begins looking for more economical lodgings.

l: chemical laboratory, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: The chemical laboratory is located in a wing of the hospital and is filled with bottles, tables, retorts, test-tubes, and Bunsen lamps. Sherlock Holmes works there on a reagent that reacts to hæmoglobin.

l: Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Baker Street is the location of a suite of rooms that Sherlock Holmes has found and believes will suit him and Dr. Watson. Holmes and Watson plan to inspect and settle the arrangements there.

l: suite of rooms, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Sherlock Holmes has his eye on a suite of rooms in Baker Street that can be shared with Dr. Watson. The two men agree to see the rooms and determine the arrangements together.

l: hæmoglobin, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Sherlock Holmes discovers a reagent that is precipitated by hæmoglobin and by nothing else. He dilutes a drop of blood in water and demonstrates the resulting reaction to Dr. Watson.

l: blood stains, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Blood stains can be difficult to distinguish from mud, rust, or fruit stains when found on clothing months after a suspected crime. Sherlock Holmes’s discovery is presented as a means of identifying them reliably, whether they are old or new.

l: Sherlock Holmes’ test, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Sherlock Holmes’ test uses a reagent that produces a mahogany colour and brownish precipitate when hæmoglobin is present. Holmes claims that it will provide a reliable medico-legal test for blood stains and could have affected numerous past criminal cases.

l: Afghanistan, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER I.
s: Afghanistan is where Dr. Watson served during the second Afghan war and was wounded at the battle of Maiwand. Holmes recognizes that Watson has been there, and Watson later reflects that he has experienced enough noise and excitement in Afghanistan to last him a lifetime.

l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Dr. John Watson moves into 221B, Baker Street, with Sherlock Holmes, and observes Holmes’s unusual habits, appearance, knowledge, and abilities. Watson learns that Holmes works as a consulting detective, applying observation, deduction, chemistry, anatomy, knowledge of crime, and other specialized skills to cases brought by official and private investigators. Holmes explains how he deduced that Watson had come from Afghanistan and correctly identifies a visitor as a retired sergeant of Marines. The chapter establishes Holmes’s confidence in the Science of Deduction and Analysis and his disdain for fictional detectives such as Dupin and Lecoq.

l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Sherlock Holmes moves into 221B, Baker Street, with Dr. John Watson and settles into a quiet, highly regular life. He reveals that he is a consulting detective who advises official and private investigators, and he demonstrates his powers of observation and deduction by identifying Watson’s past and a visitor’s former occupation.

l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Dr. John Watson moves his belongings from the hotel into 221B, Baker Street, and begins living with Sherlock Holmes. He becomes increasingly curious about Holmes, records Holmes’s areas of knowledge and ignorance, initially dismisses Holmes’s theories of deduction, and witnesses Holmes’s accurate deductions.

l: 221B Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: 221B, Baker Street consists of two comfortable bedrooms and a large, airy sitting-room with two broad windows. It becomes the shared residence of Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson and serves as Holmes’s place of business, where clients and investigators come to consult him.

l: the Science of Deduction and Analysis, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: The Science of Deduction and Analysis is described as a discipline based on long and patient study of observation and reasoning. Sherlock Holmes applies it professionally, using small physical details to infer a person’s history, occupation, and circumstances.

l: consulting detective work, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Consulting detective work is Sherlock Holmes’s occupation. Government detectives and private investigators bring him evidence or cases when they are at fault, and he studies the details, draws on his knowledge of crime, and directs them toward the correct solution.

l: observation and deduction, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Sherlock Holmes treats observation and deduction as practical skills essential to his livelihood. He explains that his reasoning about Dr. John Watson’s military and medical appearance, injuries, complexion, and recent hardships led him to conclude that Watson had come from Afghanistan.

l: The Book of Life, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: The Book of Life is an article in a magazine that argues that an observant person can infer a man’s history and profession from details such as his fingernails, clothing, boots, callosities, expression, and shirt cuffs. Dr. John Watson considers its reasoning exaggerated and impractical, while Sherlock Holmes reveals that he wrote it and relies on its principles.

l: Dr. Watson's move into 221B, Baker Street, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Dr. Watson concludes the arrangement for the rooms at 221B, Baker Street and moves his belongings from the hotel there that evening. He and Sherlock Holmes spend the next days unpacking and arranging their possessions before settling into their new surroundings.

l: Sherlock Holmes's knowledge and abilities, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Sherlock Holmes has profound knowledge of chemistry, accurate but unsystematic knowledge of anatomy, practical knowledge of geology and British law, extensive knowledge of sensational literature, and skill with the violin, singlestick, boxing, and swordsmanship. His knowledge of literature, philosophy, and astronomy is described as nil, his knowledge of politics as feeble, and his botany as variable, while his ability to distinguish poisons is strong.

l: Afghanistan, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: Afghanistan is identified by Sherlock Holmes as the place from which Dr. John Watson had recently come. Holmes reaches this conclusion by combining observations about Watson’s medical and military appearance, tropical complexion, illness, hardship, and injured left arm.

l: the retired sergeant of Marines, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER II.
s: The retired sergeant of Marines approaches 221B, Baker Street carrying a large blue envelope and looking for the correct number. Sherlock Holmes identifies him as a retired sergeant of Marines, and the man confirms that he was a sergeant in the Royal Marine Light Infantry before explaining that he is currently a commissionaire.

l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Sherlock Holmes and the Doctor travel to 3, Lauriston Gardens after Tobias Gregson’s letter reports the body of Enoch J. Drebber in an empty house. Holmes examines the scene, the body, the blood, the footprints, and the objects found in Drebber’s pockets, concluding that Drebber was murdered by poison. Lestrade discovers the blood-red inscription “RACHE,” while Holmes argues that it means “revenge” in German rather than referring to a woman named Rachel. Holmes deduces that the murderer was a tall man who arrived with Drebber in a four-wheeled cab and smoked a Trichinopoly cigar, then leaves with the Doctor to question John Rance.

l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Sherlock Holmes receives Tobias Gregson’s report and goes with the Doctor to 3, Lauriston Gardens. He examines the grounds, the body, the room, the blood, and the objects found in Enoch J. Drebber’s pockets, concluding that Drebber was murdered by poison. Holmes deduces that the murderer was a man over six feet tall, in the prime of life, with small feet, coarse square-toed boots, a florid face, long fingernails on his right hand, and a Trichinopoly cigar; he also infers that the man arrived with Drebber in a four-wheeled cab.

l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: The Doctor accompanies Sherlock Holmes to 3, Lauriston Gardens and observes the investigation and the body of Enoch J. Drebber. He reads Tobias Gregson’s letter aloud and records Holmes’s deductions about the crime.

l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Enoch J. Drebber is identified by cards found in the pockets of the dead man at 3, Lauriston Gardens. He was from Cleveland, Ohio, and appears to have been preparing to return to New York.

l: Joseph Stangerson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Joseph Stangerson’s name is found on the fly-leaf of a pocket edition of Boccaccio’s Decameron in Enoch J. Drebber’s possession. A letter addressed to Stangerson is also found among Drebber’s belongings, and Tobias Gregson has sent inquiries about him.

l: Inspector Gregson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Tobias Gregson writes to Sherlock Holmes about the body found at 3, Lauriston Gardens and meets Holmes and the Doctor at the house. He has preserved the interior but allowed the pathway to become crowded with footprints, and he reports the objects found in Enoch J. Drebber’s pockets and the inquiries sent about Joseph Stangerson.

l: Lestrade, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Lestrade participates in the investigation at 3, Lauriston Gardens. He discovers the blood-red inscription “RACHE” on the wall and interprets it as the beginning of the female name Rachel, but Holmes says it is the German word for “revenge.”

l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Sherlock Holmes states that the murderer was a man over six feet tall and in the prime of life, with small feet, coarse square-toed boots, probably a florid face, and unusually long fingernails on his right hand. Holmes says the man smoked a Trichinopoly cigar and came to 3, Lauriston Gardens with Enoch J. Drebber in a four-wheeled cab drawn by a horse with three old shoes and one new shoe on its off fore leg.

l: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: 3, Lauriston Gardens is an empty house off the Brixton Road where Enoch J. Drebber’s body is found. The house has a bare, dusty dining-room with a dirty window, a red wax candle, and a blood-red inscription on a section of exposed plaster.

l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: The murder of Enoch J. Drebber occurs during the night at 3, Lauriston Gardens. There is no wound on Drebber, but blood is scattered around the room, a woman’s wedding-ring is found beneath the body, and Sherlock Holmes concludes that poison was used.

l: Enoch Drebber's death, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Enoch J. Drebber’s death is discovered after a constable notices a light in the empty house at about two in the morning. His body shows an expression of horror and hatred, but no visible wound; Sherlock Holmes concludes that he died from poison.

l: Brixton Mystery, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: The investigation at Lauriston Gardens is conducted by Tobias Gregson and Lestrade, with Sherlock Holmes and the Doctor observing and assisting. Holmes studies the grounds and room in detail, collects grey dust, examines the inscription, and asks for the address of John Rance, the constable who found the body.

l: poisoning, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: Sherlock Holmes identifies poison as the means by which Enoch J. Drebber was killed. The text gives no further details about the poison.

l: the letter for Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: The letter from Tobias Gregson informs Sherlock Holmes that a well-dressed man has been found dead at 3, Lauriston Gardens. It identifies the man through cards bearing the name Enoch J. Drebber, reports blood in the room but no wound or apparent cause of death, and asks Holmes to come and give his opinion.

l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: A plain gold wedding-ring rolls out when Enoch J. Drebber’s body is lifted. Lestrade identifies it as a woman’s wedding-ring, which Tobias Gregson says complicates the case.

l: RACHE inscription, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: The blood-red inscription consists of the single word “RACHE,” written on exposed plaster where the wallpaper has peeled away. Lestrade believes it is the unfinished name Rachel, while Sherlock Holmes says that “Rache” is German for “revenge.”

l: the body of Enoch J. Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER III.
s: The body of Enoch J. Drebber is found lying on the bare floor of the dining-room at 3, Lauriston Gardens. Drebber is middle-aged, broad-shouldered, dressed in respectable clothing, and has clenched hands, interlocked legs, and a face marked by horror and hatred; no wound is found on him.

l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson leave No. 3, Lauriston Gardens and visit constable John Rance to obtain firsthand evidence about the murder. Holmes explains his deductions about the two suspects, identifying Patent-leathers as shorter and Square-toes as a tall, agitated man who likely returned for the ring. Rance reports finding a tall, red-faced, drunken man in a brown overcoat near the house, whom Holmes believes was the second suspect. Holmes concludes that the writing “RACHE” was a deliberate false clue and continues pursuing the mystery.

l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Sherlock Holmes explains that the cab tracks, footprints, stride lengths, writing height, fingernail marks, and cigar ash led him to deductions about the suspects. He interviews John Rance and identifies the tall, red-faced drunken man as the second suspect, believing that the man returned for the ring. Holmes plans to use the ring as bait if necessary and describes the murder as a scarlet thread to be unraveled.

l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Doctor Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes from No. 3, Lauriston Gardens to question John Rance. He remains puzzled by several aspects of the case but recognizes that Rance’s description matches Holmes’s idea of the second suspect.

l: John Rance, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: John Rance tells Holmes and Watson that he found a light and a body inside the apparently empty house in Lauriston Gardens during his night beat. He also reports encountering a tall, red-faced, extremely drunken man in a brown overcoat near the gate, whom he and Murcher had to support.

l: the first suspect (Patent-leathers), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Patent-leathers is identified through marks in the dust as one of the two people who arrived at the house by cab. He walked around a puddle rather than across it and apparently stood still while Square-toes paced and became increasingly agitated.

l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Square-toes is identified as the taller man, whose stride measured about four and a half feet and whose writing was placed just over six feet high. He crossed a puddle by hopping over it, paced excitedly while talking, and is believed to be the tall, red-faced drunken man seen by John Rance; Holmes thinks he returned for the ring.

l: No. 3, Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson leave No. 3, Lauriston Gardens after examining the scene of the murder. Holmes bases several deductions about the suspects and their movements on evidence found there.

l: Lauriston Gardens, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: The two houses in Lauriston Gardens were empty because their owner would not have the drains inspected, and the last tenant of one had died of typhoid fever. John Rance became suspicious when he saw a light in one of the houses during the night.

l: cab, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: A cab left two deep wheel ruts and distinctive hoof marks near the curb at No. 3, Lauriston Gardens. Holmes concludes that it arrived during the night and brought Patent-leathers and Square-toes to the house; Rance later reports hearing no cab after the drunken man was found.

l: the murder of Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: The murder occurred inside the empty house in Lauriston Gardens after the two suspects entered together. Holmes says that the evidence indicates Square-toes became increasingly agitated while speaking before the tragedy occurred.

l: Brixton Mystery, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Holmes says his mind is made up about the main facts of the case, though some details remain obscure. He believes the evidence provides a working basis for continuing the investigation.

l: the Drebber–Stangerson murder investigation, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Holmes says the tall, red-faced man found by John Rance holds the clue to the mystery. He intends to capture him, using the ring as bait if necessary.

l: the ring, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: The woman’s ring was found at the scene and is one of the unexplained facts troubling Doctor Watson. Holmes believes the second suspect returned to the house to recover it and may use it to catch him.

l: RACHE inscription, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER IV.
s: Holmes says that “RACHE” was a false clue intended to divert the police toward Socialism, secret societies, or a German suspect. He argues that the lettering was made by a clumsy imitator rather than a real German.

l: A Study in Scarlet, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
s: Dr. Watson and Sherlock Holmes use an advertisement about a gold wedding ring found near Brixton Road to lure the suspected murderer in the brown coat to 221B Baker Street. Instead, Mrs. Sawyer arrives claiming the ring belongs to her daughter Sally, but Holmes suspects that the old woman is a disguised accomplice. Holmes follows her to Duncan Street, where she escapes from the cab and leaves no trace. Holmes concludes that the visitor was actually a young, agile man and that the murderer has allies willing to help him.

l: Doctor Watson, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
s: Dr. Watson rests at 221B Baker Street after the Brixton Road murder but is unable to sleep because of the case. He speaks with Sherlock Holmes, prepares his service revolver, receives Mrs. Sawyer, and later waits anxiously for Holmes to return from following her.

l: Sherlock Holmes, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
s: Sherlock Holmes hypothesizes that the murderer lost the wedding ring while bending over Enoch J. Drebber’s body and places an advertisement in Dr. Watson’s name to recover it. He expects the murderer in the brown coat to respond, but instead follows the disguised visitor to Duncan Street and realizes that the apparent old woman was an agile young man.

l: Enoch Drebber, A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
s: Enoch J. Drebber’s distorted face continues to trouble Dr. Watson, who regards him as deeply vicious despite believing that justice must be done. Holmes thinks the murderer dropped a wedding ring while stooping over Drebber’s body.

l: the second suspect (Square-toes), A Study in Scarlet, CHAPTER V.
s: The murderer in the brown coat is suspected by Sherlock Holmes of having lost the wedding ring at the murder scene and of returning to the house after discovering it was missing. Holmes expects him to answer the advertisement, but the person who appears is a disguised accomplice.
